name: 大口水産 ヤキヤキコーナー (Ohguchi Suisan Yakiyaki Corner)

claims.text: Skewers are cooked on a shared open grill alongside marinated and sauced items, so cross-contact with wheat-containing sauces is likely.
Sashimi and sushi are served, which are typically eaten with standard (wheat-containing) soy sauce; no gluten-free soy sauce is documented.
Salt-grilled items such as nodoguro shioyaki and plain salted scallops are grilled simply with salt rather than sauce.

name: 近江町市場 杉本水産 近江町店 (Ohmicho Ichiba Sugimoto Suisan Ohmicho-ten)

claims.text: The kabayaki tare (basting glaze) is made with local Oono soy sauce and malt syrup, and the eel is repeatedly coated with it during grilling — standard soy sauce is wheat-based, so the signature product contains gluten.
The shop is entirely a fish and shellfish operation (eel, loach, fresh seafood, winter crab); no plant-based options are offered and all grilling equipment is used for fish.

name: 近江町市場寿し (Omicho Ichiba Zushi)

claims.text: Conveyor-belt sushi setting with shared belts, soy sauce dispensers, and prep surfaces makes cross-contact with wheat highly likely; no gluten-free handling is documented.
Standard Japanese soy sauce (wheat-containing) is the default condiment for nigiri and donburi here; no wheat-free tamari is documented.
The kitchen is seafood-centric with shared rice and surfaces; no vegan preparation is documented and cross-contact with fish is unavoidable.
Wheat ramen noodles (slender straight noodles by Kanno Seimen) are the base of every bowl, so the kitchen handles wheat throughout; no gluten-free preparation is documented.
The shoyu ramen is built on a soy-sauce tare; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat and there is no indication of a wheat-free alternative.

All broths are animal-based (nodoguro fish bones, oyster oil, duck and chicken), and toppings include pork chashu and egg, so vegan diners cannot be accommodated and cross-contact with seafood and meat is unavoidable.
English and Chinese menus are available, which helps foreign visitors identify ingredients before ordering.

name: 近江町食処 鮮彩えにし (Omicho Shokusho Sensai Enishi)

claims.text: Sashimi bowls, sushi and the hitsumabushi are served and eaten with soy sauce, which standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat; no wheat-free soy alternative is documented.
The kitchen is a dedicated seafood operation run by a fish wholesaler; all signature dishes are fish or shellfish, so cross-contact with animal products is unavoidable.
English and Korean menus are available, which can help diners ask about ingredients.
Traditional Kaga kaiseki and Japanese cuisine of this style is built on dashi and wheat-based Japanese soy sauce; no gluten-free soy sauce or alternative is documented.
Courses are seafood- and meat-inclusive (sashimi, scallop and squid, white fish, crab, beef hot pot), prepared with fish dashi; no vegan preparation is documented.
Nigiri is brushed with nikiri (a soy-sauce-based glaze) before serving, and standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat — there is no indication of a gluten-free alternative.
The entire omakase is built around fish, shellfish, and seafood from the Noto Peninsula, with no plant-based course described.
Full-menu café that also serves pizza, gratin and doria — wheat dishes share the kitchen and copper griddle with the rice-flour pancake; no cross-contamination protocol is mentioned.

The GF curry base is a house 「かえし醤油」 (kaeshi soy sauce). Kaeshi is made from ordinary shōyu, which normally contains wheat; the shop only claims 小麦粉 (wheat flour) is absent and does not state a tamari/GF soy sauce, so celiac-safety of the curry is unconfirmed.
Rice-flour pancake contains egg and whipped butter; not vegan.
No published allergen-handling or celiac protocol found; wheat-free claim is worded around 小麦粉 (wheat flour) only.
Explicit 米粉100% pancake and a 「小麦粉・化学調味料・保存料一切不使用」 curry — a rare wheat-free lunch option in Arimatsu.
